kicker: MLR570 · a visual guide to our survey
title: Non-Convex Optimization in Neural Networks: from saddle escape to the edge of stability
lede: A visual journey through our survey, section by section. It starts with the math every later section needs, built from scratch. It then follows the survey's single thread: gradient descent multiplies every curvature direction by $1-\eta\lambda$. It leaves saddles when $\lambda<0$ and lives at the edge of stability when $\lambda>2/\eta$. Every visual is explained: what the axes are, what moves, and what to notice. Every surface is a real function; every ball runs a real optimizer.

parts.title: Introduction
parts.blurb: Why training non-convex networks should be hard, why it works anyway, and the two research questions of the survey.

parts.title: Mathematical preliminaries
parts.blurb: The loss, gradients and Hessians, flat points and what counts as success, the assumptions behind the theorems, the algorithms, and the one multiplier that connects the two halves of the survey.

parts.title: Escaping saddles (RQ1)
parts.blurb: What plain gradient descent and SGD do near saddle points: they almost never stop there, they can wait a very long time, noise helps, and from small initialization the saddles are stages of learning.

parts.title: Beyond the stability threshold (RQ2)
parts.blurb: What happens when the step size is too large for the curvature: catapults, the edge of stability, why training survives, central flows, and the adaptive and stochastic versions.

parts.title: Critical comparison
parts.blurb: The two halves side by side: one instability of the gradient-descent map, two faces.

parts.title: Open problems and conclusion
parts.blurb: Gaps between what is proved and what is observed, and the take-away of the survey.

chapters.title: The puzzle and the plan
chapters.question: Training a network means minimizing a non-convex loss, which is NP-hard in the worst case. Why does plain gradient descent work, and which part of that question does our survey answer?

chapters.title: From a network to a loss, and its local shape
chapters.question: What exactly is being minimized, why is it non-convex, and how do the gradient and the Hessian describe the loss near a point?

chapters.title: Flat points, success, and assumptions
chapters.question: Where the gradient vanishes, how do we tell a minimum from a saddle, what does it mean for an algorithm to succeed, and what do the theorems assume about the loss?

chapters.title: The algorithms under study
chapters.question: What do GD, SGD, momentum, Adam and Newton's method actually do in one step, and why is Newton's method drawn to saddles?

chapters.title: One multiplier: linear stability and 2/η
chapters.question: Near a critical point, gradient descent multiplies each curvature direction by 1 − ηλ. What do the three regimes of this one number mean, and how do they connect the two halves of the survey?

chapters.title: Saddles: why they matter, and why GD almost never stops at one
chapters.question: Saddles outnumber minima in high dimension, and depth makes some of them degenerate. Why does gradient descent from a random start converge to a strict saddle with probability zero?

chapters.title: Avoidance is not efficiency; noise as the way out
chapters.question: If GD avoids saddles, can it still waste exponential time near them? How do random perturbations and SGD's own noise make escape fast?

chapters.title: Saddles as stages of learning
chapters.question: From small initialization, training starts at a saddle and moves from one saddle to the next. Why are these plateaus a feature rather than a bug?

chapters.title: Before the edge: stability of SGD, the break-even point, catapults
chapters.question: Which minima can SGD with a given step size and batch size stay in, and what happens when the step size is larger than the curvature allows?

chapters.title: The edge of stability
chapters.question: Real networks trained by full-batch gradient descent push their sharpness up to 2/η and then hover there, while the loss keeps falling. What exactly is observed, and what does it break?

chapters.title: Why it does not blow up
chapters.question: Past 2/η the linear analysis predicts divergence. Which mechanism keeps training alive, and where has it been proved?

chapters.title: Central flows: the time-averaged trajectory
chapters.question: The iterates oscillate wildly at the edge of stability. Can we describe their average path instead, and what does that description predict?

chapters.title: Beyond full-batch GD: Adam, warmup, SAM, SGD, and where training ends
chapters.question: Do adaptive methods, sharpness-aware updates and minibatch SGD have their own edges of stability, and how do large steps change which minimum training reaches?

chapters.title: One instability, two faces
chapters.question: Strict saddles and too-sharp minima are both unstable fixed points of the gradient-descent map. How do the two literatures compare, and what do their theorems assume?

chapters.title: Open problems and the take-away
chapters.question: Where does the evidence run out, which questions does that leave open, and what is the survey's conclusion?
